To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Coasian propositions are supported in a setting with incomplete information and economic rules of liability.

(1) the voluntary bargaining solution is efficient; (2) the voluntary bargaining process is neutral in the sense that the bargaining solution does not depend on the initial distribution of the gains from trade; (3) the bargaining process is affected by altruism, reciprocity, and other social preferences; and (4) the bargaining process can be affected by the institutional framework, in particular by liability rules.

(i) the Coasian efficiency proposition holds in a voluntary externality setting with incomplete information and economic rules, and (ii) the Coasians’ neutrality proposition holds only for the long-run.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the voluntary approach to the externality problem and the Coasian proposition that a bargaining solution will be reached in the absence of transaction costs.
the voluntary approach to the resolution of externality problems.
the question of how well the Coasian theory of externalities holds up in the laboratory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the experimental results provide strong support for the efficiency proposition but not for the neutrality proposition.
Coase's theory of the firm is a useful tool for analyzing the efficiency of the voluntary approach to externailty problems.
Coasian propositions are supported by experimental results, and that the voluntary approach to externaility problems may be an effective and efficient way to deal with such problems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the experimental results are generally consistent with the theoretical Coasian propositions and with the predictions of the economic theory of bargaining.
the Coasian propositions are not always supported by the experimental data but that they are not refuted either.
the Coase theorem is supported, and that it holds in the presence of liability rules, incomplete information, and with a large number of agents.

, in the presence of incomplete information, economic liability rules are more likely to achieve the Coasean efficiency than legal liability rules.
the Coasian approach can be a viable approach to externality resolution, but it is not a panacea for all problems.
